title: £4.45m of payments worth a closer look.
summary: I narrowed a noisy duplicate-payment check into a review list for Accounts Payable, then found a separate risk in how personal payments were published.
audience: Finance, Accounts Payable and Information Governance
metrics: possible duplicate payment pairs worth £4.45m flagged for review
source: Published council payments over £500; project management summary and SQL outputs.
brief: A finance team needs two different things from a payments report: a credible explanation of spending changes and a manageable list of exceptions to investigate. I used 247,785 payment lines, covering £3.87bn, to build both. This is an independent portfolio exercise using published data, rather than work commissioned by the council.
finding: A standard duplicate rule returned 6,553 pairs. Many were repeated care-package rates, so treating every match as a problem would waste review time. I added a one-off-amount condition: the same amount of at least £1,000, for the same supplier, within three days, appearing exactly twice across the dataset. That left 281 candidate pairs, including 73 on the same day.
decision: Start with the 73 same-day pairs and check invoice references in the finance system. The £4.45m is an exception-review amount, not a confirmed loss or a saving I delivered. Published payment records alone cannot distinguish duplicate invoices from legitimate payments or publication duplicates.
methods: Cleaned and standardised supplier and directorate fields, mapping 18 source directorate names into stable reporting groups.
Built a SQLite star schema with payments as the fact table and separate supplier, date, directorate and category dimensions.
Combined corporate directorates affected by the September 2025 restructure so budget transfers did not appear as genuine changes in spending.
Compared 1 April to 23 July in both years. A partial July should not be compared with a complete month.
Kept personal-payment reporting aggregated and pseudonymised individual supplier identifiers in the analysis outputs.
secondary_title: The spending increase needs a timing check.
secondary: Year-to-date payments rose from £559m to £677m, a 21% increase. Birmingham Highways payments were £88m against £21m a year earlier, with a £12m credit requiring reconciliation. I would confirm the PFI schedule with City Operations before interpreting this as a lasting change. Separately, agency spending rose from £34m to £43m over the matched period.
actions: Accounts Payable
Review the candidate pairs against invoices, beginning with same-day matches; validate and resolve duplicate supplier records.
City Operations
Reconcile the highways payment schedule and credit before briefing on year-to-date pressure.
Information Governance
Review supplier identifiers on redacted individual payments. Twelve identifiers linked to names elsewhere in the published data; this site publishes only the aggregate finding.
limitations: Payments show cash outflow by payment date, not commitments, service costs or budget variance.
Invoice references are absent. Possible duplicates require confirmation; candidate pairs are not proven overpayments.
35% of FY2025/26 spend uses the generic PO accrual category, limiting category-level interpretation.
Supplier-number and personal-name details are deliberately excluded from the website.
reflection: The useful output was a more selective review rule. A large exception count can look impressive while creating little practical value for the team expected to check it.

highlight.headline: Explaining expenses and flagging payments for review
highlight.situation: Birmingham City Council’s published payment records show spending information, but changes in department names, repeated payment amounts and limited invoice details make it difficult to interpret how the money was spent.
highlight.task: Prepare a spending summary and flag payment exceptions for the finance manager or Accounts Payable team to investigate.
highlight.action: I processed 247,785 payment records, standardised department names and developed a SQL reporting model. I compared spending across equivalent periods and refined the duplicate-payment rules to reduce false positives from legitimate recurring transactions.
highlight.results: I flagged 281 possible duplicate payment pairs worth £4.45m, including 73 same-day pairs. I also identified a privacy risk affecting 213 redacted payments, which could be linked to names elsewhere in the published records.
highlight.implications: Accounts Payable can prioritise the same-day pairs and check invoices before confirming any overpayments. Information Governance should review how supplier identifiers appear alongside redacted payments. The flagged amount represents potential exceptions, not confirmed losses.
highlight.key_label: possible duplicate payment pairs worth £4.45m flagged for review

title: Average satisfaction hides a relationship gap.
summary: Platform matches its large-landlord peers overall. The breakdown points to weaker communication and listening, alongside repairs figures that need checking.
audience: Housing association board and performance team
metrics: tenants satisfied with communication, compared with similar large landlords
source: Regulator of Social Housing TSM data; Housing Ombudsman reports; project benchmarking pack.
brief: A board needs to know where service improvement should focus, and whether the comparisons are fair. I benchmarked Platform against 17 large housing associations with at least 40,000 homes, then added complaint outcomes from 21 Midlands landlords. The two peer groups answer different questions and are kept separate.
finding: Overall satisfaction is 64.6%, up about two percentage points and exactly at the large-landlord median. That average conceals shortfalls in communal areas, information, neighbourhood contribution and listening. My priorities combine the gaps with the measures most closely associated with overall satisfaction: listening and acting, keeping tenants informed, and maintaining homes.
decision: Ask management for an improvement plan with named owners and measures for communication and listening. Keep the apparent repairs decline provisional until the underlying recording change is explained. These are recommendations from an independent analysis, rather than actions implemented by Platform.
methods: Selected large housing associations as the main TSM peer group; comparing with smaller landlords would introduce a known size effect.
Compared measure-level results with peer medians and quartiles rather than relying on a single satisfaction score.
Used cross-landlord correlations to inform prioritisation alongside Platform’s own performance gaps.
Extracted Ombudsman tables from 21 PDF reports and checked category totals against the headline findings.
Checked annual changes against the underlying counts and reporting definitions before treating them as service changes.
secondary_title: A repairs decline that needs a denominator check.
secondary: Non-emergency repairs completed within target fell from a rounded 92% to 62%. Over the same period, recorded repairs fell from 90,250 to 13,872 despite the same 28-day target. This suggests a comparability problem worth investigating; it does not establish that the entire performance decline is a recording artefact. ASB and complaint volumes also need definition checks.
actions: Resident engagement
Track how tenant feedback leads to decisions, and report back to tenants on what changed.
Performance reporting
Confirm repairs, ASB and complaint definitions before using the annual movements in a board paper.
Repairs leadership
Review the well-maintained-home gap alongside repairs complaints, rather than assuming prompt complaint responses mean the underlying service is resolved.
limitations: Cross-landlord correlation describes association; it does not establish what causes satisfaction to improve.
Survey method, sample composition and local conditions can affect comparisons, even within a size-based peer group.
Ombudsman cases are an escalated subset of complaints, not a measure of every tenant’s experience.
Four extracted Ombudsman reports reconcile within one or two findings because a category label could not be read. The detailed decisions note records this limitation.
reflection: Choosing a relevant comparison group changed the story. Platform was around the large-landlord average, while the measure-level gaps still gave the board specific issues to investigate.

highlight.headline: Comparing tenant satisfaction and identifying service priorities
highlight.situation: Platform’s overall satisfaction score offers a broad view of tenant experience, but conceals differences between services. Comparisons with smaller landlords can also distort its relative performance.
highlight.task: Benchmark Platform against similar-sized housing associations, identify improvement priorities and check unusual changes before preparing a board report.
highlight.action: I benchmarked satisfaction measures against 17 large housing associations and extracted Ombudsman findings for 21 Midlands landlords. I examined gaps in individual measures, compared complaint outcomes and checked annual movements against the underlying reporting volumes.
highlight.results: Platform’s overall satisfaction was 64.6%, in line with similar large landlords. For every 100 tenants, around seven fewer were satisfied with communication and five fewer felt listened to. Recorded repair volumes fell sharply alongside reported repairs performance, so I flagged the figures for checks before drawing conclusions.
highlight.implications: Management should prioritise communication, listening and home maintenance. The performance team should confirm reporting definitions before presenting the repairs decline as a straightforward change in service quality.
highlight.key_label: tenants satisfied with communication, compared with similar large landlords

title: Fewer spills. A drier year. Progress to examine.
summary: Reported spills fell 41%. I checked rainfall and monitor reliability before identifying the sites that still warrant operational review.
audience: Environmental performance, maintenance and investment teams
metrics: Midlands rainfall over the same period
overflows with at least 60 spills in 2025
source: Environment Agency EDM returns; st_yearly_summary.csv; project performance pack.
brief: The performance team needs a defensible account of the annual change and clear exception lists for maintenance and investment. I combined six years of Environment Agency returns, normalised changing file formats and checked whether falling spill totals reflected weather, monitoring or a change in performance.
finding: Spills fell from 62,085 to 36,471 while Midlands rainfall fell from about 1,000 mm to 717 mm. A simple model attributes roughly half of the reduction to rainfall, but that estimate is indicative. A useful cross-check is 2022: rainfall was similar to 2025, and the average spills per reliably monitored overflow were about 23% lower in 2025 than in 2022.
decision: Report spills alongside rainfall and monitor coverage. Investigate the remaining high-spilling sites, beginning with those without a reported improvement action. Similar annual rainfall is a useful comparison, but differences in storm intensity, local conditions and asset changes remain.
methods: Normalised monitor operation from fractions and percentages, and converted several duration formats into decimal hours.
Matched changing overflow identifiers across years using the old-format ID field.
Calculated trend averages using monitors operating for at least 90% of the year so missing observation time did not masquerade as better performance.
Used spills per overflow as well as totals because the reporting population changes between years.
Kept the rainfall model simple and compared similar-rainfall years as a separate sense check.
secondary_title: The average improvement leaves concentrated risks.
secondary: Seventy-six overflows still recorded at least 60 spills in 2025, including 58 in the Trent basin. Thirteen had no improvement action reported. Storm tanks at treatment works represent 13% of overflows but account for 47% of spill hours, making them a useful starting point for asset-level review.
actions: Maintenance
Prioritise the 27 monitors reported below 90% operation in both 2024 and 2025.
Investment and operations
Review the 13 high-spilling overflows without a reported improvement action, then investigate the wider high-spill group.
Reporting
Show rainfall, observation coverage and changes in the reporting population alongside annual spill totals.
limitations: Annual regional rainfall is a coarse proxy for event-level catchment conditions. Weather adjustment is not causal proof.
Reliably monitored groups can change composition between years; they are not automatically a fixed matched panel.
The management summary lists 87 low-uptime monitors in 2025; the yearly CSV lists 90. The site avoids presenting either as a reconciled total. The denominator needs checking before publication.
The 2021 overflow-level totals differ from the EA summary by eight spills and seven hours; this small discrepancy is recorded in the data-quality log.
reflection: A favourable headline needs the same scrutiny as a poor one. Better monitor coverage also changes what is observed, so I made that part of the interpretation rather than treating it as background detail.

highlight.headline: Assessing sewage-spill reductions and prioritising sites for review
highlight.situation: Severn Trent reported fewer sewage spills in 2025, but lower rainfall may explain part of the improvement. Gaps in monitoring can also understate spills when sensors fail to record events.
highlight.task: Assess the reported improvement, account for rainfall and monitoring coverage, and identify sites requiring maintenance or investment review.
highlight.action: I combined six years of environmental returns, standardised file formats and checked monitor reliability. I compared spill trends with rainfall, examined years with similar rainfall and identified sites with persistent spills or recurring monitor failures.
highlight.results: Reported spills fell 41%, while regional rainfall fell 28%. Across reliably monitored sites, average spills were approximately 23% lower in 2025 than in 2022, a year with similar rainfall. However, 76 sites recorded at least 60 spills in 2025, including 13 without a reported improvement action.
highlight.implications: Managers should report spill reductions alongside rainfall and monitoring coverage, then prioritise the remaining high-spill sites for review. Similar annual rainfall strengthens the comparison but does not isolate the effects of engineering improvements or local weather conditions.
highlight.key_label: sites with at least 60 spills in 2025

title: March’s recovery is under pressure again.
summary: The waiting list grew 7.5% after March 2026. Referrals rose while completed pathways stayed broadly flat, making the next milestone harder to reach.
audience: Chief operating officer and elective performance team
source: NHS England RTT extracts; project performance summary, key figures and report workbook.
brief: A monthly elective-care report should explain performance against milestones, emerging pressures and where to investigate next. I processed 41 monthly NHS England extracts for UHB, six large Midlands peer trusts and England. Counts refer to RTT pathways; they should not automatically be read as unique people.
finding: UHB reached 68.6% within 18 weeks in March 2026, above the stated 65% milestone. By August it was 66.6%, while the list had grown from 89,544 to 96,303. In April–August, clock starts rose from 115,481 to 133,091; clock stops moved only from 103,997 to 104,806. This shows growing demand pressure alongside broadly flat completed activity. It does not establish that capacity is sufficient.
decision: Review referrals and completed pathways together, with a specialty-level recovery plan. The analysis estimates around 1,550 additional clock stops a month to stabilise the list under its assumptions. That is a planning estimate to reconcile with the full stock-flow balance, rather than a guaranteed delivery target.
methods: Read 41 monthly extracts and aggregated commissioner-level rows to trust and specialty level.
Checked for missing submissions and unknown clock-start dates across the selected series.
Caught an extract-schema problem: the Part 2 Total column was blank. Summed the weekly time bands and checked against Total All.
Compared UHB with six other large Midlands trusts and England, keeping local and national comparisons visible.
Back-tested a demand-and-capacity model and a trend model against a simple no-change baseline before presenting an outlook.
secondary_title: The most elaborate forecast was less accurate.
secondary: The demand-and-capacity model had 8.4% back-test error and the trend model 6.07%, compared with 2.5% for a no-change baseline. Both models missed the turn around March 2026. I would present the roughly 107,000 March 2027 list as a continuation scenario and refresh it monthly, with assumptions shown explicitly.
actions: Elective performance
Refresh starts, stops and the list balance monthly, including removals and adjustments. Investigate the recent demand increase with commissioners.
Specialty leadership
Review ENT and Ophthalmology, which account for 110 of 175 remaining 52-week waits. Investigate Gynaecology’s 38% annual list growth and 45.9% 18-week performance.
Planning
Use the March 2027 continuation scenario alongside a baseline and capacity assumptions. Check milestones against current NHS planning guidance.
limitations: Clock stops include completed pathways such as treatments and discharges; they are not a direct measure of theatre productivity.
Starts minus stops alone does not fully reconcile the waiting-list stock. Other removals and reporting adjustments must be considered.
Size-based peers do not ensure identical specialty mix, local demand or patient complexity.
The models failed their back-test relative to the baseline. The outlook is a scenario, and the published milestones require checking against current planning guidance.
reflection: Reporting that a simple baseline beat my models made the analysis more useful. A planning audience needs to understand the conditions under which an outlook might be wrong.

highlight.headline: Explaining waiting-list growth and assessing future pressure
highlight.situation: UHB improved its waiting-time performance by March 2026. By August, its waiting list had grown and fewer pathways met the 18-week standard.
highlight.task: Explain the renewed pressure, identify specialty-level concerns and assess whether forecasting could support recovery planning.
highlight.action: I processed 41 months of NHS reporting, checked completeness and reconciled reporting fields. I compared UHB with six large Midlands trusts and England, examined referrals and completed pathways, and tested two forecasting methods against a no-change baseline.
highlight.results: The waiting list grew 7.5% between March and August 2026. Referrals increased approximately 15% year on year during April–August, while completed pathways remained broadly flat. Both forecasting methods produced larger back-test errors than the simple baseline.
highlight.implications: The performance team should investigate rising referrals alongside available capacity and specialty pressures. Planners should treat the March 2027 estimate as a conditional scenario, refresh its assumptions monthly and retain the baseline comparison.
